newsitem.title: USA: Feisty Dole promises victory despite Clinton lead.
newsitem.headline: Feisty Dole promises victory despite Clinton lead.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole charged into the home-stretch of the Nov. 5 election campaign on Thursday with Clinton looking unbeatable but Dole full of fight and proclaiming, "We're going to win."

As if to show himself undaunted after a final campaign debate in which he clearly failed to land any knockout blow, Dole remained in California to woo voters in a political treasure-trove state where Clinton holds a wide lead.

While many analysts say the 73-year-old Republican is wasting valuable campaign funds by fighting on in places like this, Dole scoffed at such pessimism in a feisty appearance before laughing, cheering supporters in Riverside.

"I can't help but be amused at the way President Clinton has been sort of taking California for granted. He thinks that just because the White House has Hollywood on its side that that makes California Clinton country," Dole said. "But ... on Nov. 5 America will declare that its Dole-Kemp country.
"We're going to win," he said to rousing cheers, and got more by telling the crowd that "on Wednesday morning, Nov. 6, Bill Clinton will be the most surprised man in America."
"Thats why we're in California and thats why we're coming back to California," he said.

Clinton, now sitting on national polling leads ranging from high single-digits to the upper teens, brimmed with confidence too after a strong Wednesday night debate performance but told a rally in Santa Ana, California that his Democrats must ensure a good voter turn-out on Nov. 5
"The big question in 19 days is, who's going to show up," the president said. "It's your responsibility to go vote, your responsibility as a citizen, your responsibility to be there."

A California poll published on Wednesday by the San Francisco Examiner put Clinton up on Dole statewide by 49-37 percent with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and the Green Party's Ralph Nader at three percent each.

On a nationwide basis, Thursday's daily Reuters tracking poll, which traces trends over a three-day average sample among about 900 likely voters, showed Dole moving up slightly to about 12 points behind Clinton in a sampling that did not reflect Wednesday evenings debate performances.
Clinton led Dole in the Reuters/Zogby poll by 45 percent to 33.1 percent with 6.3 percent favouring Perot. Dole trailed by about 13 percent on Wednesday.
While other surveys give Clinton slightly bigger or smaller leads, no presidential candidate in modern U.S. history has overcome any such gaps so late in a campaign.

In the celebrated Harry Truman upset of front-runner Thomas Dewey in the 1948 White House race -- a breathtaking comeback often cited by Dole partisans -- Truman only trailed Dewey by about five percentage points in mid-October.

Some Republicans in fact have given up the ghost on Dole and fret about a Clinton rout so vast it might sweep his Democrats back into control of Congress -- which they lost just two years ago -- as well.

The latest Reuters poll, like others suggests a potential for that. About 39 percent of respondents said they would vote for a Democratic candidate for Congress while slightly less than 33 percent said they would back a Republican.
The Democratic lead showed in both houses, although most polls and analysts rate their chances stronger in the House of Representatives than in the Senate.

In Wednesday's debate, Dole's strategy was to hit Clinton's ethics, credibility and performance in office and he did so at every opportunity while Clinton ignored him and touted his record on a strong U.S. economy, lowering crime rate and other positive news.

An ABC News Poll of 567 registered voters said 55 percent thought Clinton won, 28 percent thought Dole did and 14 percent called it even. The poll said the debate changed few minds although Clinton's support grew slightly.
"Dole ... inflicted a couple of flesh wounds but Clinton will put on a couple of band-aids and it will be over," said John Pitney, a political scientist at Claremont McKenna College in California.
"It's over unless something happens -- a real blockbuster that suddenly falls from the sky," said Professor Daniel Hallin of the University of California at San Diego.
